lessons.title: past -ed
lessons.art_alt: Crumb the baker dragon writes in a diary next to a fresh cake in Candy Village

hook.text: Crumb the baker dragon keeps a diary. Yesterday was busy! But Crumb wrote: “Yesterday I bake a cake and I play with Puffbun.” Hmm, that sounds like today. Can you fix the diary?
hook.say: Crumb the baker dragon keeps a diary. Yesterday was busy! But Crumb wrote: “Yesterday I bake a cake and I play with Puffbun.” Hmm, that sounds like today. Can you fix the diary?

discover.text: Stamp ed on the things that happened yesterday. Not every word needs it! You can drag the stamp or tap a word.
discover.hint: Did it happen yesterday? Stamp ed! After can or will, the verb stays plain.

items.why: Bake already ends in e, so just add d: baked.
Yesterday: we played.
After can, the verb stays plain: can swim.
Stop is short, so double the p: stopped.
Yesterday: she jumped.
Will is for later, and the verb stays plain: will clean.

discover.say: Stamp ed on the things that happened yesterday. Not every word needs it! You can drag the stamp or tap a word.

rule.text: To talk about yesterday or last week, add -ed to the doing word: play becomes played. If it ends in e, just add d: baked. Short words like stop and hop double the last letter: stopped, hopped.
examples: The bus stopped at the shop.
rule.say: To talk about yesterday or last week, add -ed to the doing word: play becomes played. If it ends in e, just add d: baked. Short words like stop and hop double the last letter: stopped, hopped.
sayEx: Crumb baked a cake yesterday.
We played in the park.
The bus stopped at the shop.

check.q: Yesterday Crumb ___ a big cake.

notes.bakes: Bakes is for every day. Yesterday needs baked.
notes.bakeed: Bake already ends in e. Just add d: baked.

check.explain: Yesterday: Crumb baked a big cake.
check.say: Yesterday Crumb blank a big cake.

check.q: Last night the bus ___ at the candy shop.

notes.stoped: Stop is a short word, so double the p: stopped.
notes.stops: Stops is for every day. Last night: stopped.

check.explain: Double the p: the bus stopped.
check.say: Last night the bus blank at the candy shop.

check.q: Which sentence is about yesterday?
options: We can played in the park.

Play with no -ed is for now or every day.
After can, the verb stays plain: can play.

check.explain: Played has the -ed, so it already happened.
check.say: Which sentence is about yesterday?

reteach.text: Here's another way. The -ed is a little time machine! Stick it on a doing word and the word zooms back to yesterday. Two spelling tricks: an e at the end just needs a d, and a short word like hop gets a double letter.

discover.text: Time machine! Stamp ed to send these words back to yesterday.
discover.hint: Like ends in e: just d. Hop and clap are short: double the last letter.

items.why: Like ends in e: liked.
Short word, double the p: hopped.
After can, the verb stays plain: can dance.
Short word, double the p: clapped.
Yesterday: you looked.

discover.say: Time machine! Stamp ed to send these words back to yesterday.

reteach.say: Here's another way. The -ed is a little time machine! Stick it on a doing word and the word zooms back to yesterday. Two spelling tricks: an e at the end just needs a d, and a short word like hop gets a double letter.

check2.q: Last week we ___ our room.

notes.cleaning: Cleaning needs is or was in front of it. Last week: cleaned.
notes.clean: Clean is for now. Last week: cleaned.

check2.explain: Last week is finished: we cleaned our room.
check2.say: Last week we blank our room.

check2.q: Puffbun ___ over the fence yesterday.

notes.hoped: Hoped comes from hope, which means to wish! For hop, double the p: hopped.
notes.hops: Hops is for every day. Yesterday: hopped.

check2.explain: Hop is short, so double the p: hopped.
check2.say: Puffbun blank over the fence yesterday.

check2.q: Which word is spelled right?

notes.likeed: Like already ends in e. Just add d: liked.
notes.likked: Like ends in e, so no double letter. Just add d: liked.

check2.explain: Like ends in e, so just add d: liked.
check2.say: Which word is spelled right?

lessons.grown: 👪 Past simple, regular verbs (A2 Key). Spelling: final -e → add -d (baked); consonant doubling after a short stressed vowel (stop → stopped); can / will + bare infinitive as the contrast. -y → -ied (cry → cried) and the /t/ /d/ /ɪd/ endings are met in practice, not taught here.

lessons.title: went, ate, saw
lessons.art_alt: Hoot the owl reads a funny diary page while Sumi the fox giggles in a candy shop

hook.text: Hoot stamped -ed on EVERY word in the diary: “I goed to the shop and I eated a lollipop!” Sumi giggles. That sounds funny! Some words don't want a stamp. Let's find them.
hook.say: Hoot stamped -ed on EVERY word in the diary: “I goed to the shop and I eated a lollipop!” Sumi giggles. That sounds funny! Some words don't want a stamp. Let's find them.

discover.text: Sort the yesterday words. Does the word just add -ed, or does it change into a new word? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.
discover.hint: Look at the end. Played has -ed. Went is a whole new word!

items.why: Play just adds -ed: played.
Go changes into a new word: went.
Eat changes into a new word: ate.
Jump just adds -ed: jumped.
See changes into a new word: saw.
Cook just adds -ed: cooked.
Have changes into a new word: had.
Walk just adds -ed: walked.

discover.say: Sort the yesterday words. Does the word just add -ed, or does it change into a new word? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.

rule.text: Most doing words add -ed for yesterday. But some special words change into a new word: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, have becomes had. We learn these by heart, like the names of friends!
examples: Yesterday I went to the shop.
rule.say: Most doing words add -ed for yesterday. But some special words change into a new word: go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, have becomes had. We learn these by heart, like the names of friends!
sayEx: Yesterday I went to the shop.
Hoot ate a lollipop.
We saw a rainbow.

check.q: Yesterday we ___ to the beach.

notes.goed: Go is a special word. Goed isn't a word: say went.
notes.go: Go is for now. Yesterday: went.

check.explain: Go is special: yesterday we went.
check.say: Yesterday we blank to the beach.

check.q: Last night Sumi ___ three cookies.

notes.eated: Eat is a special word. Eated isn't a word: say ate.
notes.eats: Eats is for every day. Last night: ate.

check.explain: Eat is special: Sumi ate three cookies.
check.say: Last night Sumi blank three cookies.

check.q: Which sentence is right?
options: I saw a big cat yesterday.
I seed a big cat yesterday.
I see a big cat yesterday.

See is a special word. Seed isn't its past: say saw.
See is for now. Yesterday: saw.

check.explain: See is special: I saw a big cat.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Say the special words like a little song: go, went. Eat, ate. See, saw. Have, had. Come, came. If a word with -ed sounds silly, like goed or eated, it's a special word!

discover.text: Sing it, then drag the special word into each gap. You can also tap a word.
discover.hint: go → went, eat → ate, see → saw, come → came.

items.why: Go is special: went.
Eat is special: ate.
See is special: saw.
Come is special: came.

discover.say: Sing it, then drag the special word into each gap. You can also tap a word.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Say the special words like a little song: go, went. Eat, ate. See, saw. Have, had. Come, came. If a word with -ed sounds silly, like goed or eated, it's a special word!

check2.q: Hoot ___ a new hat last week.

notes.haved: Have is a special word. Haved isn't a word: say had.
notes.has: Has is for now. Last week: had.

check2.explain: Have is special: Hoot had a new hat.
check2.say: Hoot blank a new hat last week.

check2.q: Grandma ___ to visit us last Sunday.

notes.comed: Come is a special word. Comed isn't a word: say came.
notes.comes: Comes is for every week. Last Sunday: came.

check2.explain: Come is special: Grandma came last Sunday.
check2.say: Grandma blank to visit us last Sunday.

check2.q: Which past word just adds -ed?

notes.went: Went is a new word for go. It has no -ed.
notes.ate: Ate is a new word for eat. It has no -ed.

check2.explain: Play just adds -ed: played.
check2.say: Which past word just adds -ed?

lessons.grown: 👪 Past simple, irregular verbs (A2 Key list: go/went, eat/ate, see/saw, have/had, come/came). Saying goed or eated is a normal stage of learning: praise the try, then say the right form back.

lessons.title: bigger, more beautiful

match.re: comparative|-er to compare|-er \+ than|→ \w+er than|→ \w+er\. Example:.* than|more \+ adjective \+ than|good → better

lessons.art_alt: Puffbun and Sumi race along a candy path while Crumb holds two cakes, one small and one big

hook.text: It's race day in Candy Village! Puffbun is fast. Sumi is even faster! Then Crumb shows two cakes. One is beautiful, and the other is… beautifuller? That sounds silly! How do we compare two things?
hook.say: It's race day in Candy Village! Puffbun is fast. Sumi is even faster! Then Crumb shows two cakes. One is beautiful, and the other is… beautifuller? That sounds silly! How do we compare two things?

discover.text: Stamp er on the short words. Long words use more instead! Drag the stamp or tap a word.
discover.hint: Clap the word. One clap (tall, big) → er. Lots of claps (beau-ti-ful) → no stamp.

items.why: Tall is short: taller.
Big is short, so double the g: bigger.
Beautiful is long, so it uses more: more beautiful.
Nice ends in e, so just add r: nicer.
Small is short: smaller.
Expensive is long, so it uses more: more expensive.

discover.say: Stamp er on the short words. Long words use more instead! Drag the stamp or tap a word.

rule.text: To compare two things, short words add -er: tall becomes taller, big becomes bigger, nice becomes nicer. Long words use more: more beautiful. Then add than: Sumi is faster than Puffbun.
examples: A lion is bigger than a cat.
This cake is more beautiful than that one.
rule.say: To compare two things, short words add -er: tall becomes taller, big becomes bigger, nice becomes nicer. Long words use more: more beautiful. Then add than: Sumi is faster than Puffbun.
sayEx: Sumi is faster than Puffbun.
A lion is bigger than a cat.
This cake is more beautiful than that one.

check.q: A lion is ___ than a cat.

notes.more big: Big is short, so it takes -er: bigger.
notes.biggest: Biggest is for the top one of a group. Two animals: bigger than.

check.explain: Big is short: a lion is bigger than a cat.
check.say: A lion is blank than a cat.

check.q: This dress is ___ than that one.

notes.beautifuller: Beautiful is long, so no -er. Say more beautiful.
notes.beautifullest: That isn't a word. For two things: more beautiful than.

check.explain: Beautiful is long: more beautiful than.
check.say: This dress is blank than that one.

check.q: Which sentence is right?
options: Sumi is more fast than Puffbun.

Fast is short, so it takes -er: faster.
To compare, use than, not that.

check.explain: Short word + -er + than: faster than.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Clap the word! One clap, like fast or hot, gets -er. Words that end in y, like happy, change the y to i: happier. Lots of claps, like dan-ger-ous, get more in front. And one special word: good becomes better!

discover.text: Clap and stamp! Stamp er on the words that take it.
discover.hint: Happy and funny: y becomes i. Hot: double the t. Long words: no stamp.

items.why: Happy ends in y: happier.
Hot is short, so double the t: hotter.
Dangerous is long, so it uses more: more dangerous.
Funny ends in y: funnier.
Interesting is long, so it uses more: more interesting.

discover.say: Clap and stamp! Stamp er on the words that take it.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Clap the word! One clap, like fast or hot, gets -er. Words that end in y, like happy, change the y to i: happier. Lots of claps, like dan-ger-ous, get more in front. And one special word: good becomes better!

check2.q: Today is ___ than yesterday.

notes.hoter: Hot is short, so double the t: hotter.
notes.more hot: Hot is short, so it takes -er: hotter.

check2.explain: Double the t: today is hotter.
check2.say: Today is blank than yesterday.

check2.q: My cat is ___ than my dog.

notes.happyer: Happy ends in y. Change y to i, then -er: happier.
notes.more happy: We usually say happier, because happy ends in y.

check2.explain: y becomes i: happier than.
check2.say: My cat is blank than my dog.

check2.q: My new book is ___ than my old one.

notes.interestinger: Interesting is long, so no -er. Say more interesting.
notes.interesting: We are comparing two books, so we need more … than.

check2.explain: Long word: more interesting than.
check2.say: My new book is blank than my old one.

lessons.grown: 👪 Comparative adjectives (A2 Key): one syllable + -er (doubling big → bigger, -e → -r), two syllables ending in -y → -ier, longer adjectives more + adjective, followed by than. Irregular good → better is introduced; bad → worse is met in practice.

lessons.title: the biggest
lessons.art_alt: Crumb the baker dragon at a cake show with three cakes in a row, the tallest one wearing a gold ribbon

hook.text: It's the Candy Village Cake Show! Crumb baked three cakes: a big one, a bigger one, and one that is bigger than ALL the others. What should the gold ribbon say?
hook.say: It's the Candy Village Cake Show! Crumb baked three cakes: a big one, a bigger one, and one that is bigger than ALL the others. What should the gold ribbon say?

discover.text: Make the gold ribbons! Stamp est on the short words. Long words use the most instead. Drag the stamp or tap a word.
discover.hint: Short word → the + est. Long word (lots of claps) → no stamp, say the most.

items.why: The number one: the tallest.
Big is short, so double the g: the biggest.
Delicious is long, so it uses the most: the most delicious.
Nice ends in e, so just add st: the nicest.
The number one: the smallest.
Beautiful is long, so it uses the most: the most beautiful.

discover.say: Make the gold ribbons! Stamp est on the short words. Long words use the most instead. Drag the stamp or tap a word.

rule.text: To pick the number one in a group, use the and add -est: the tallest, the biggest, the nicest. Long words use the most: the most beautiful.
examples: It's the most delicious cake in the show!
rule.say: To pick the number one in a group, use the and add -est: the tallest, the biggest, the nicest. Long words use the most: the most beautiful.
sayEx: This is the biggest cake.
Sumi is the fastest fox.
It's the most delicious cake in the show!

check.q: Sumi is the ___ fox in Candy Village.

notes.faster: Faster compares only two. The number one of all: the fastest.
notes.most fast: Fast is short, so it takes -est: the fastest.

check.explain: The number one: the fastest fox.
check.say: Sumi is the blank fox in Candy Village.

check.q: This is the ___ cake in the shop!

notes.deliciousest: Delicious is long, so no -est. Say the most delicious.
notes.more delicious: More is for two things. The number one: the most delicious.

check.explain: Long word: the most delicious.
check.say: This is the blank cake in the shop!

check.q: Which sentence is right?
options: Puffbun is the most small bunny.

Small is short, so it takes -est: the smallest.

check.explain: the + short word + est: the smallest.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of a prize podium with steps. Step one: tall. Step two, comparing two: taller. The top step, the winner of everyone: the tallest. The top step always has the. And good is special: good, better, the best!

discover.text: Two things or the top of all? Drag each card into its step, or tap a card and then a step.
discover.hint: Than means two things. The … -est means the winner of everyone.

items.why: Than compares two: taller than.
The number one in class: the tallest.
Than compares two: bigger than.
Of all means the winner: the biggest.
Good, better, the best: the top.
Than compares two: better than.

discover.say: Two things or the top of all? Drag each card into its step, or tap a card and then a step.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of a prize podium with steps. Step one: tall. Step two, comparing two: taller. The top step, the winner of everyone: the tallest. The top step always has the. And good is special: good, better, the best!

check2.q: It's 35 degrees! This is the ___ day of the year.

notes.hotest: Hot is short, so double the t: hottest.
notes.most hot: Hot is short, so it takes -est: the hottest.

check2.explain: Double the t: the hottest day.
check2.say: It's 35 degrees! This is the blank day of the year.

check2.q: We laughed and laughed. That was the ___ film ever!

notes.funnyest: Funny ends in y. Change y to i, then -est: funniest.
notes.most funny: We usually say the funniest, because funny ends in y.

check2.explain: y becomes i: the funniest film.
check2.say: We laughed and laughed. That was the blank film ever!

check2.q: Hoot got 10 out of 10. That's the ___ score!

notes.goodest: Good is special: good, better, the best.
notes.most good: Good is special. We never say most good: the best.

check2.explain: Good is special: the best score.
check2.say: Hoot got 10 out of 10. That's the blank score!

lessons.grown: 👪 Superlative adjectives (A2 Key): the + adjective + -est / the most + longer adjective; spelling as for comparatives (biggest, nicest, funniest); irregular good → best. Usually followed by in / of (the tallest in the class).

lessons.title: going to: plans

match.re: going to (for|=|\+)|be going to|going to \+ verb

lessons.art_alt: Gumdrop pins drawings of a cake, balloons and music onto a party plan board while Puffbun holds a balloon

hook.text: Gumdrop is planning a party for Saturday! She made a plan board, but the words fell off. “I ___ bake a cake. Puffbun ___ bring balloons.” Can you put the plan back together?
hook.say: Gumdrop is planning a party for Saturday! She made a plan board, but the words fell off. “I blank bake a cake. Puffbun blank bring balloons.” Can you put the plan back together?

discover.text: Drag the right plan words into each gap, or tap a tile. Look at who is doing it!
discover.hint: I → am going to. He, she, it, one name → is going to. We, they, two names → are going to.

items.why: I goes with am: I am going to bake.
One friend goes with is: Puffbun is going to bring balloons.
We goes with are: we are going to dance.
One friend goes with is: Crumb is going to make lemonade.

items.s: Hoot and Sumi ___ sing a song.
items.why: Two friends go with are: they are going to sing.

discover.say: Drag the right plan words into each gap, or tap a tile. Look at who is doing it!

rule.text: When you have a plan for later, say am, is or are, then going to, then the plain doing word. I am going to bake. She is going to swim. They are going to play. We often say it short: I'm going to.
examples: I'm going to visit Grandma on Sunday.
Puffbun is going to bring balloons.
We are going to have a party!
rule.say: When you have a plan for later, say am, is or are, then going to, then the plain doing word. I am going to bake. She is going to swim. They are going to play. We often say it short: I'm going to.
sayEx: I'm going to visit Grandma on Sunday.
Puffbun is going to bring balloons.
We are going to have a party!

check.q: Tomorrow I ___ visit my grandma.

notes.going to: It needs am in front: I am going to visit.
notes.am going: Don't forget to: I am going to visit.

check.explain: A plan: I am going to visit my grandma.
check.say: Tomorrow I blank visit my grandma.

check.q: Sumi ___ play football on Saturday.

notes.are going to: Sumi is one friend, so use is: Sumi is going to play.
notes.is going to plays: After going to, the doing word stays plain: play, not plays.

check.explain: One friend + is going to + plain word: Sumi is going to play.
check.say: Sumi blank play football on Saturday.

check.q: Which sentence is a plan for tomorrow?
options: We are going to swim tomorrow.
We are going to swam tomorrow.

Swam is for yesterday. After going to, use the plain word: swim.
A piece is missing! We need are: we are going to swim.

check.explain: All three pieces are there: are + going to + swim.
check.say: Which sentence is a plan for tomorrow?

reteach.text: Here's another way. A plan is like a little train with three carriages. Carriage one: am, is or are. Carriage two: going to. Carriage three: the plain doing word, like swim or play. If a carriage is missing, the train can't go! We also use going to when we can see something is about to happen: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain!
examples: ☁️ Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.

discover.text: Check each plan train. Is it ready to go, or does it need fixing? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.
discover.hint: Look for all three carriages: am / is / are, then going to, then a plain word like play.

items.why: All three carriages: am + going to + read.
Carriage one is missing: she is going to swim.
All three carriages: are + going to + play.
The last word must be plain: he is going to eat.
All three carriages: are + going to + cook.
I goes with am: I am going to sing.

discover.say: Check each plan train. Is it ready to go, or does it need fixing? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.

reteach.say: Here's another way. A plan is like a little train with three carriages. Carriage one: am, is or are. Carriage two: going to. Carriage three: the plain doing word, like swim or play. If a carriage is missing, the train can't go! We also use going to when we can see something is about to happen: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain!

check2.q: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.

notes.are going to: It is one thing, so use is: it is going to rain.
notes.going to: A carriage is missing! It needs is: it is going to rain.

check2.explain: We can see the clouds, so it is going to rain.
check2.say: Look at those dark clouds! It blank rain.

check2.q: My brothers ___ watch a film tonight.

notes.is going to: Brothers means more than one, so use are.
notes.am going to: Am only goes with I. My brothers are going to watch.

check2.explain: More than one person: my brothers are going to watch a film.
check2.say: My brothers blank watch a film tonight.

check2.q: What ___ you going to do on Sunday?

notes.is: You goes with are: what are you going to do?
notes.do: Going to questions use am, is or are, not do: what are you going to do?

check2.explain: In a question, are jumps to the front: What are you going to do?
check2.say: What blank you going to do on Sunday?

lessons.grown: 👪 be going to + bare infinitive for plans and intentions (A2 Key), plus predictions from present evidence (Look at those clouds!). Contrast with will (next lesson): going to = decided before; will = promises, offers and guesses. Watch for the missing auxiliary (She going to…), the commonest error.

lessons.title: will: promises and guesses
lessons.art_alt: Hoot looks into a pink candy crystal ball while Sumi offers Puffbun a new ice-cream cone

hook.text: At the Candy Village market, Hoot looks into a candy crystal ball: “I think it will be sunny tomorrow!” Then Puffbun drops her ice cream. Sumi says: “Don't cry. I'll buy you a new one!” They both used will. But they mean different things. Can you sort them?
hook.say: At the Candy Village market, Hoot looks into a candy crystal ball: “I think it will be sunny tomorrow!” Then Puffbun drops her ice cream. Sumi says: “Don't cry. I'll buy you a new one!” They both used will. But they mean different things. Can you sort them?

discover.text: Is it a promise or a kind offer, or is it a guess about later? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.
discover.hint: A promise or offer means: I'll do it for you. A guess often has I think, maybe or probably.

items.t: I'll buy you a new one!
items.why: Sumi offers to do something kind: a promise or offer.

items.t: I think it will be sunny.
items.why: I think tells us it's a guess.

items.t: I won't tell anyone. I promise!
items.why: I promise tells us: it's a promise.

items.t: Maybe Sumi will win the race.
items.why: Maybe tells us it's a guess.

items.t: I'll carry your bag for you.
items.why: A kind offer to help: I'll carry it.
Probably tells us it's a guess.

discover.say: Is it a promise or a kind offer, or is it a guess about later? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.

rule.text: Will helps us talk about later. We use it to make a promise or a kind offer: I'll help you! And we use it to guess: I think it will rain. After will, the doing word stays plain. Will not is won't. I will is often I'll.
examples: I'll help you with your bag.
rule.say: Will helps us talk about later. We use it to make a promise or a kind offer: I'll help you! And we use it to guess: I think it will rain. After will, the doing word stays plain. Will not is won't. I will is often I'll.
sayEx: I'll help you with your bag.
I won't forget, I promise!
I think Puffbun will win.

check.q: Don't worry, I ___ help you with your homework.

notes.wills: Will never takes -s: I will, she will, we will.
notes.am will: Will doesn't need am. Just say I will help.

check.explain: A kind offer: I will help you.
check.say: Don't worry, I blank help you with your homework.

check.q: I think Puffbun will ___ the race.

notes.wins: After will, the doing word stays plain: will win.
notes.won: Won is for yesterday. After will, use the plain word: win.

check.explain: A guess: will + plain word, will win.
check.say: I think Puffbun will blank the race.

check.q: Which one is a promise?
options: Maybe the bus will be late.

I think shows it's a guess about the weather, not a promise.
Maybe shows it's a guess, not a promise.

check.explain: I won't forget means I promise to remember.
check.say: Which one is a promise?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Will is a word that never changes. I will, you will, she will, they will: no s, no am, no is. The word after it stays plain. Put your hand on your heart for a promise. Look into a crystal ball for a guess. When you say no, will not becomes won't.
examples: 🤝 I'll call you later, I promise.

discover.text: Will or won't? Drag the right word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: Won't means will not. Read the whole sentence first!

items.s: I ___ tell your secret. I promise!
items.why: Keeping a secret means you will NOT tell: won't.

items.s: I think it ___ be sunny tomorrow.
items.why: A happy guess: it will be sunny.

items.s: Hoot is sick, so he ___ come to school.
items.why: He is sick, so he will NOT come: won't.

items.s: Your bag looks heavy. I ___ carry it.
items.why: A kind offer: I will carry it.

discover.say: Will or won't? Drag the right word into each gap, or tap it.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Will is a word that never changes. I will, you will, she will, they will: no s, no am, no is. The word after it stays plain. Put your hand on your heart for a promise. Look into a crystal ball for a guess. When you say no, will not becomes won't.

check2.q: My sister ___ be ten next year.

notes.wills: Will never takes -s, even after my sister.
notes.is will: Will doesn't need is. Just say she will be.

check2.explain: Will never changes: my sister will be ten.
check2.say: My sister blank be ten next year.

check2.q: Sumi doesn't like chocolate. I think she ___ eat the cake.

notes.will: She doesn't like chocolate, so the guess is no: she won't eat it.
notes.doesn't will: We never put doesn't with will. Will not is won't.

check2.explain: A no guess: she won't (will not) eat the cake.
check2.say: Sumi doesn't like chocolate. I think she blank eat the cake.

check2.q: Puffbun says, “I'm thirsty!” Which is a kind offer?
options: I will to get you some water.

For an offer, add will: I'll get you some water.
No to after will: I will get, not I will to get.

check2.explain: I'll (I will) + get: a kind offer.
check2.say: Puffbun says, “I'm thirsty!” Which is a kind offer?

lessons.grown: 👪 will + bare infinitive for promises, offers, spontaneous decisions and predictions with I think / maybe / probably (A2 Key); won't = will not. Contrast with be going to (plans, evidence). Common errors: wills, will to, am will.

lessons.title: some or any?

match.re: any in questions|Some in offers|There isn't any|Is there any…|some eggs in a yes

lessons.art_alt: Crumb the baker dragon looks into a cupboard with a basket of eggs, an empty shelf and an empty flour sack

hook.text: Crumb wants to bake cookies. He opens the cupboard and talks to himself: “There are some eggs. But is there any flour? Oh no, there isn't any sugar!” Some or any? Let's find out when to use each one.
hook.say: Crumb wants to bake cookies. He opens the cupboard and talks to himself: “There are some eggs. But is there any flour? Oh no, there isn't any sugar!” Some or any? Let's find out when to use each one.

discover.text: Which word fits the gap: some or any? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.
discover.hint: Look at the end of the sentence. A question mark or a not word (isn't, aren't, don't) → any. A yes sentence → some.

items.why: A yes sentence: there are some eggs.
A question: is there any flour?
A not sentence (isn't): there isn't any sugar.
A yes sentence: I have some butter.
A question: are there any cherries?
A not sentence (don't): we don't have any milk.

discover.say: Which word fits the gap: some or any? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a basket.

rule.text: Use some in yes sentences: There are some eggs. Use any in questions and not sentences: Is there any flour? There isn't any sugar. One more thing: when you offer something or ask for it nicely, use some: Would you like some cake?
examples: There are some eggs in the cupboard.
rule.say: Use some in yes sentences: There are some eggs. Use any in questions and not sentences: Is there any flour? There isn't any sugar. One more thing: when you offer something or ask for it nicely, use some: Would you like some cake?
sayEx: There are some eggs in the cupboard.
Is there any flour?
Would you like some juice?

check.q: There are ___ apples in the basket.

notes.any: This is a yes sentence, so use some.
notes.a: A is for one thing. Apples means more than one: some apples.

check.explain: A yes sentence: there are some apples.
check.say: There are blank apples in the basket.

check.q: We don't have ___ bread.

notes.some: Don't makes it a not sentence, so use any.
notes.a: We don't say a bread. In a not sentence: any bread.

check.explain: A not sentence (don't): we don't have any bread.
check.say: We don't have blank bread.

check.q: Which sentence is right?

Aren't makes it a not sentence, so use any.
Sweets means more than one, so use aren't.

check.explain: Not sentence + more than one: there aren't any sweets.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Some is a sunny yes word. Any is a curious word: it loves question marks and not words like isn't and don't. So look for a question mark or a not word. If you find one, use any. But when you ask nicely or offer, like Can I have… or Would you like…, use some.
examples: 🙏 Can I have some water, please?

discover.text: Some or any? Drag the word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: A question mark or a not word → any. Yes sentences and asking nicely → some.

items.s: There aren't ___ pencils in my bag.
items.why: Aren't is a not word: any pencils.
Asking nicely with please: some water.
A question: any pets?
A yes sentence: some grapes.

discover.say: Some or any? Drag the word into each gap, or tap it.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Some is a sunny yes word. Any is a curious word: it loves question marks and not words like isn't and don't. So look for a question mark or a not word. If you find one, use any. But when you ask nicely or offer, like Can I have… or Would you like…, use some.

check2.q: Hoot hasn't got ___ brothers.

notes.some: Hasn't makes it a not sentence, so use any.
notes.a: Brothers means more than one, so not a.

check2.explain: A not sentence (hasn't): any brothers.
check2.say: Hoot hasn't got blank brothers.

check2.q: I'm hungry. Can I have ___ biscuits, please?

notes.any: When we ask for something nicely, we use some.
notes.a: Biscuits means more than one, so not a.

check2.explain: Asking nicely: can I have some biscuits?
check2.say: I'm hungry. Can I have blank biscuits, please?

check2.q: Are there ___ ducks in the pond?

notes.a: Ducks means more than one, so not a.
notes.much: We can count ducks, so much doesn't fit. Questions use any.

check2.explain: A question: are there any ducks?
check2.say: Are there blank ducks in the pond?

lessons.grown: 👪 some / any with plural countable and uncountable nouns (A2 Key): some in affirmatives, offers and requests (Would you like some…? Can I have some…?); any in questions and negatives. The something/anything family comes later.

lessons.title: much or many?

match.re: How many is|How many \+|'much' with|Much for things|Many for things|much with milk

lessons.art_alt: Sumi stands at her candy shop counter with a jar of sweets and a jug of strawberry milk while Puffbun points at the jar

hook.text: Sumi opens her candy shop. Puffbun asks: “How many sweets can I have?” Gumdrop asks: “How much milk is in the jug?” Why many for sweets, but much for milk? Let's sort the shop!
hook.say: Sumi opens her candy shop. Puffbun asks: “How many sweets can I have?” Gumdrop asks: “How much milk is in the jug?” Why many for sweets, but much for milk? Let's sort the shop!

discover.text: Can you count it one by one? Drag each card into the right jar, or tap a card and then a jar.
discover.hint: Try saying a number in front: three sweets works! Three milks? No, milk is poured, not counted.

items.why: You can count sweets: one, two, three. How many sweets?
You pour milk, you can't count it one by one. How much milk?
You can count apples. How many apples?
Water can't be counted one by one. How much water?
You can count cookies. How many cookies?
Sugar is too tiny to count one by one. How much sugar?
You can count eggs. How many eggs?
Rice grains are too tiny to count. How much rice?

discover.say: Can you count it one by one? Drag each card into the right jar, or tap a card and then a jar.

rule.text: Things you can count one by one, like sweets and apples, use many: How many sweets? Things you can't count, like milk, water, sugar and rice, use much: How much milk? We use much and many mostly in questions and not sentences.
examples: How many sweets are in the jar?
How much milk is in the jug?
rule.say: Things you can count one by one, like sweets and apples, use many: How many sweets? Things you can't count, like milk, water, sugar and rice, use much: How much milk? We use much and many mostly in questions and not sentences.
sayEx: How many sweets are in the jar?
How much milk is in the jug?
There isn't much sugar.

check.q: How ___ apples do you want?

notes.much: You can count apples, so use many.
notes.lot: We don't say how lot. Things you can count: how many.

check.explain: We can count apples: how many apples?
check.say: How blank apples do you want?

check.q: How ___ milk is in the jug?

notes.many: You can't count milk one by one, so use much.
notes.lot: We don't say how lot. Things you can't count: how much.

check.explain: We can't count milk: how much milk?
check.say: How blank milk is in the jug?

check.q: Which sentence is right?

Water can't be counted, so use much, not many.
Water is one big amount, so use isn't, not aren't.

check.explain: Water can't be counted: there isn't much water.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way: the number test. Put a number in front of the word. Three cookies? Yes! So it's many. Three milks? That sounds funny. We say three glasses of milk. So milk is much. Many goes with the s words you can count. Much goes with things you pour, scoop or sprinkle.
examples: 🥛 a glass of milk → How much milk?

discover.text: Much or many? Try the number test, then drag the word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: Can you say three in front? Yes → many. No → much.

items.why: Three cars works: how many cars?
Three rices sounds funny: how much rice?
We can't count time one by one: much time.
Three chairs works: not many chairs.

discover.say: Much or many? Try the number test, then drag the word into each gap, or tap it.

reteach.say: Here's another way: the number test. Put a number in front of the word. Three cookies? Yes! So it's many. Three milks? That sounds funny. We say three glasses of milk. So milk is much. Many goes with the s words you can count. Much goes with things you pour, scoop or sprinkle.

check2.q: How ___ eggs do we need for the cake?

notes.much: You can count eggs, so use many.
notes.lot: We don't say how lot. Things you can count: how many.

check2.explain: Three eggs works: how many eggs?
check2.say: How blank eggs do we need for the cake?

check2.q: We haven't got ___ sugar.

notes.many: Sugar can't be counted one by one, so use much.
notes.a: We don't say a sugar here. Not much sugar.

check2.explain: Sugar can't be counted: we haven't got much sugar.
check2.say: We haven't got blank sugar.

check2.q: Which one can you count one by one?

notes.water: You pour water. You can't count it one by one.
notes.juice: You pour juice. You can't count it one by one.

check2.explain: One cookie, two cookies: you can count cookies.
check2.say: Which one can you count one by one?

lessons.grown: 👪 Countable vs uncountable nouns with much / many and How much / How many? (A2 Key). In affirmatives English prefers a lot of / lots of (lots of milk, lots of sweets); much and many are mostly used in questions and negatives. How much is it? for prices is met in the shopping lesson.

lessons.title: always … never
lessons.art_alt: Hoot the owl in round glasses points at a weekly sticker chart with toothbrush, broccoli and book pictures and rows of gold stars, while Puffbun, a pink-and-mint fluffy pet, waves

hook.text: Puffbun has a sticker chart! Every day she does something, she gets a gold star. Hoot points at it: “Look! Lots of stars under the toothbrush, fewer under the book, and one row is still empty!” How do we say how often Puffbun does things? Let's put the words in order.
hook.say: Puffbun has a sticker chart! Every day she does something, she gets a gold star. Hoot points at it: “Look! Lots of stars under the toothbrush, fewer under the book, and one row is still empty!” How do we say how often Puffbun does things? Let's put the words in order.

discover.text: Each star is one day of the week. Put each how-often word on its step: drag it, or tap a word and then a step.
discover.hint: Start at the ends! Always has all 7 stars at the top. Never has no stars at the bottom.

items.why: Always means every time: 7 days out of 7.
Usually means nearly every time: 6 days out of 7.
Often means lots of times: about 4 days out of 7.
Sometimes means just a few times: about 2 days out of 7.
Never means not one time: 0 days out of 7.

discover.say: Each star is one day of the week. Put each how-often word on its step: drag it, or tap a word and then a step.

rule.text: How often do you do it? Always means every time. Usually means nearly every time. Often means lots of times. Sometimes means a few times. Never means not one time. These words sit just before the doing word: I always brush my teeth. But they come after am, is or are: Hoot is never late.
examples: Hoot is never late for school.
rule.say: How often do you do it? Always means every time. Usually means nearly every time. Often means lots of times. Sometimes means a few times. Never means not one time. These words sit just before the doing word: I always brush my teeth. But they come after am, is or are: Hoot is never late.
sayEx: Puffbun always brushes her teeth.
I sometimes read before bed.
Hoot is never late for school.

check.q: Puffbun brushes her teeth every single day. She ___ brushes her teeth.

notes.sometimes: Sometimes is only a few days. Every day is always.
notes.never: Never means not one day. She brushes every day!

check.explain: Every day, all 7 stars: always.
check.say: Puffbun brushes her teeth every single day. She blank brushes her teeth.

check.q: Which sentence is right?

With is, the how-often word comes after it: is never late.
The how-often word doesn't go at the end. Say: is never late.

check.explain: After is comes the how-often word: Hoot is never late.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

check.q: Sumi eats broccoli on 2 days a week. She ___ eats broccoli.

notes.always: Always would be every day, all 7.
notes.never: Never would be 0 days, but she eats it on 2 days.

check.explain: Just a few days, like 2 out of 7: sometimes.
check.say: Sumi eats broccoli on 2 days a week. She blank eats broccoli.

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of a glass of juice. Always is a full glass. Usually is nearly full. Often is more than half. Sometimes is a little splash. Never is an empty glass! Where does the word sit? Just before the doing word: I often swim. But after am, is or are: She is always kind.

discover.text: Count the days, then drag the right how-often word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: 7 days → always. 6 → usually. About 4 → often. About 2 → sometimes. 0 → never.

items.s: (7 of 7 days) Gumdrop ___ waters her flowers.
items.why: Every day: always.
Not one day: never.
Just a few days: sometimes.

items.s: (6 of 7 days) Sumi ___ walks to school.
items.why: Nearly every day: usually.
Lots of days, but not nearly all: often.

discover.say: Count the days, then drag the right how-often word into each gap, or tap it.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of a glass of juice. Always is a full glass. Usually is nearly full. Often is more than half. Sometimes is a little splash. Never is an empty glass! Where does the word sit? Just before the doing word: I often swim. But after am, is or are: She is always kind.

check2.q: Gumdrop helps her friends every day. She is ___ kind.

notes.never: She helps every day, so never doesn't fit.
notes.sometimes: Every day is more than a few times: always.

check2.explain: Every day: she is always kind.
check2.say: Gumdrop helps her friends every day. She is blank kind.

check2.q: Which sentence is right?
options: We often go to the beach.
We go to often the beach.
We often to go the beach.

The how-often word sits just before the doing word: often go.
The words are mixed up. Say: we often go to the beach.

check2.explain: How-often word, then the doing word: we often go.
check2.say: Which sentence is right?

check2.q: How often do you eat cabbage? — ___. I don't like it!

notes.Always: If you don't like it, you won't eat it every time!
notes.Usually: Usually is nearly every time. You don't like it, so: never.

check2.explain: Not one time: never.
check2.say: How often do you eat cabbage? — blank. I don't like it!

lessons.grown: 👪 Adverbs of frequency (A2 Key): always > usually > often > sometimes > never, with How often…? Position: before the main verb (I often swim) but after be (She is always late). Hardly ever / rarely come later (B1). The discovery uses a new 'order on a line' ladder: days out of 7, like the sticker chart.

lessons.title: must, have to, mustn't

match.re: mustn't|don't have to|it's necessary|have to \+ verb

lessons.art_alt: Hoot in a park-keeper cap stands at the Candy Village playground gate beside three picture signs: a bike helmet, a crossed-out ice cream and a sweet wrapper going into a bin, while Puffbun the white bunny and Sumi the fox look up

hook.text: Hoot is the park keeper today! At the playground gate there are three picture signs: a bike helmet, an ice cream with a big red cross, and a sweet wrapper going into a bin. Puffbun and Sumi ask: “What do the signs mean?” Let's sort the playground rules!
hook.say: Hoot is the park keeper today! At the playground gate there are three picture signs: a bike helmet, an ice cream with a big red cross, and a sweet wrapper going into a bin. Puffbun and Sumi ask: “What do the signs mean?” Let's sort the playground rules!

discover.text: Is it a rule to DO, or a rule NOT to do? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a sign box.
discover.hint: ✅ must = you need to do it. ⛔ mustn't = don't do it, it isn't allowed.

items.t: wear a helmet on your bike
items.why: The helmet sign says: you must wear a helmet.

items.t: eat ice cream in the playground
items.why: The ice cream has a cross: you mustn't eat it here.
The bin sign says: you must put wrappers in the bin.
Climbing the fence isn't safe: you mustn't.
The gate keeps little ones safe: you must close it.
Litter makes the park dirty: you mustn't drop it.

discover.say: Is it a rule to DO, or a rule NOT to do? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a sign box.

rule.text: Must means you need to do it, it's a rule: You must wear a helmet. Have to means the same: You have to wear a helmet. Mustn't means don't do it, it isn't allowed: You mustn't climb the fence. But be careful! Don't have to means you don't need to, but you can if you want.
examples: She has to wear a helmet.
We don't have to go to school on Sunday.
rule.say: Must means you need to do it, it's a rule: You must wear a helmet. Have to means the same: You have to wear a helmet. Mustn't means don't do it, it isn't allowed: You mustn't climb the fence. But be careful! Don't have to means you don't need to, but you can if you want.
sayEx: You must close the gate.
She has to wear a helmet.
You mustn't drop litter.
We don't have to go to school on Sunday.

check.q: You ___ climb the fence. It isn't safe!

notes.must: Must would mean you need to climb it! It isn't safe, so: mustn't.
notes.don't have to: Don't have to means you can if you want. Climbing isn't allowed, so: mustn't.

check.explain: Not allowed: you mustn't climb the fence.
check.say: You blank climb the fence. It isn't safe!

check.q: Sumi ___ wear a helmet when she rides her bike.

notes.have to: Sumi is one friend, so use has to.
notes.has: It needs to as well: Sumi has to wear a helmet.

check.explain: One friend: has to + the plain doing word.
check.say: Sumi blank wear a helmet when she rides her bike.

check.q: It's Saturday! We ___ go to school today.

notes.mustn't: Mustn't would mean school is not allowed! It just isn't needed today: don't have to.
notes.must: There's no school on Saturday, so we don't need to go.

check.explain: Not needed today: we don't have to go.
check.say: It's Saturday! We blank go to school today.

reteach.text: Here's another way: traffic lights. Must and have to are green: go and do it! Mustn't is red: stop, don't do it. Don't have to is yellow: you choose. You can, but you don't need to. With he, she or one name, have to becomes has to: Hoot has to lock the gate.
examples: 🟢 Hoot has to lock the gate.
🔴 You mustn't feed the ducks sweets.
🟡 It's sunny. You don't have to wear a coat.

discover.text: Green, red or yellow? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: 🟢 needs to → has to. 🔴 not allowed → mustn't. 🟡 not needed, you choose → don't have to.

items.s: Hoot ___ lock the gate at night.
items.why: It's Hoot's job, so he needs to: has to.

items.s: You ___ feed the ducks sweets. It makes them ill.
items.why: It hurts the ducks, so it isn't allowed: mustn't.

items.s: It's sunny. You ___ wear a coat.
items.why: A coat isn't needed, but you can wear one: don't have to.

items.s: Puffbun ___ wash her hands before lunch.
items.why: One friend who needs to: has to.
Shouting isn't allowed in the library: mustn't.

discover.say: Green, red or yellow? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

reteach.say: Here's another way: traffic lights. Must and have to are green: go and do it! Mustn't is red: stop, don't do it. Don't have to is yellow: you choose. You can, but you don't need to. With he, she or one name, have to becomes has to: Hoot has to lock the gate.

check2.q: Crumb, you ___ touch the hot oven!

notes.don't have to: Don't have to means you can choose. Touching a hot oven is never OK: mustn't.
notes.must: Must would mean you need to touch it. Ouch! Say mustn't.

check2.explain: Dangerous, so not allowed: mustn't.
check2.say: Crumb, you blank touch the hot oven!

check2.q: My brother ___ get up early. He has football at 8.

notes.have to: My brother is one person, so use has to.
notes.must to: No to after must. Say must get up, or has to get up.

check2.explain: One person who needs to: has to.
check2.say: My brother blank get up early. He has football at 8.

check2.q: Which sentence means you can choose?
options: You don't have to bring a pen.

Mustn't means a pen is not allowed. That's not a choice.
Must means you need a pen. That's not a choice either.

check2.explain: Don't have to: you don't need to, but you can.
check2.say: Which sentence means you can choose?

lessons.grown: 👪 Obligation and prohibition (A2 Key): must / have to (has to with he, she, it) for rules and things that are necessary; mustn't = not allowed; don't have to = not necessary. The classic trap is mustn't ≠ don't have to. Common errors: must to, she have to.

lessons.title: should: good advice
lessons.art_alt: Puffbun the white bunny is wrapped in a mint blanket with a cold while Hoot the owl gives gentle advice and Sumi the fox offers a mug of honey drink and a striped scarf

hook.text: Oh dear, Puffbun has a cold! She's wrapped up in her mint blanket, sniffing. Hoot and Sumi want to help. Sumi brings a warm honey drink and a stripy scarf. What should Puffbun do to get better? Let's give her some good advice.
hook.say: Oh dear, Puffbun has a cold! She's wrapped up in her mint blanket, sniffing. Hoot and Sumi want to help. Sumi brings a warm honey drink and a stripy scarf. What should Puffbun do to get better? Let's give her some good advice.

discover.text: Good idea, or not a good idea? Drag should or shouldn't into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: Will it help Puffbun get better? Yes → should. No → shouldn't.

items.why: A warm drink helps: you should drink it.

items.s: You ___ go out in the rain.
items.why: Rain makes a cold worse: you shouldn't go out.
A scarf keeps you warm: you should wear it.
You need lots of sleep: you shouldn't stay up late.
Resting helps you get better: you should rest.

discover.say: Good idea, or not a good idea? Drag should or shouldn't into each gap, or tap it.

rule.text: When we give advice, we say should. It means: this is a good idea. You should rest. Shouldn't means: this is not a good idea. You shouldn't go out in the rain. After should, use the plain doing word, with no to and no s: She should drink water.
examples: You shouldn't eat ice cream today.
Puffbun should go to bed early.
rule.say: When we give advice, we say should. It means: this is a good idea. You should rest. Shouldn't means: this is not a good idea. You shouldn't go out in the rain. After should, use the plain doing word, with no to and no s: She should drink water.
sayEx: You should drink something warm.
You shouldn't eat ice cream today.
Puffbun should go to bed early.

check.q: Your shoes are muddy. You ___ take them off at the door.

notes.shouldn't: Taking muddy shoes off is a good idea, so use should.
notes.should to: No to after should: you should take them off.

check.explain: A good idea: you should take them off.
check.say: Your shoes are muddy. You blank take them off at the door.

check.q: Puffbun has a cold. She should ___ lots of water.

notes.drinks: After should, the doing word stays plain: drink, not drinks.
notes.to drink: No to after should: should drink.

check.explain: Should + the plain word: she should drink.
check.say: Puffbun has a cold. She should blank lots of water.

check.q: It's very hot and sunny. Which is good advice?
options: You should wear a thick coat.

On a hot day, water is a great idea! That's bad advice.
A thick coat on a hot day would make you far too hot.

check.explain: A hat keeps the sun off your head: good advice.
check.say: It's very hot and sunny. Which is good advice?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Should is like a kind friend whispering a tip. Hoot doesn't say you must. He says you should: it's your choice, but it's a good idea. Should never changes: I should, she should, they should. No s, no to. To ask for advice, put should first: What should I do?
examples: 💬 He shouldn't eat so many sweets.

discover.text: Check each tip. Does it sound right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.
discover.hint: Look at the word after should. It stays plain: no s and no to.

items.why: Should + a plain word: should rest.
Should never takes s: he should go home.
No to after should: you should eat soup.
Shouldn't + a plain word: shouldn't shout.
The word after should stays plain: should wear.
Asking for advice: should comes first.

discover.say: Check each tip. Does it sound right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Should is like a kind friend whispering a tip. Hoot doesn't say you must. He says you should: it's your choice, but it's a good idea. Should never changes: I should, she should, they should. No s, no to. To ask for advice, put should first: What should I do?

check2.q: I've lost my library book. What ___ I do?

notes.do should: To ask for advice, just put should first: What should I do?

check2.explain: Asking for advice: What should I do?
check2.say: I've lost my library book. What blank I do?

check2.q: Hoot's tummy hurts. He ___ eat so many sweets!

notes.should: His tummy hurts, so more sweets is not a good idea: shouldn't.
notes.should to: No to after should, and here it's a bad idea: shouldn't eat.

check2.explain: Not a good idea: he shouldn't eat so many sweets.
check2.say: Hoot's tummy hurts. He blank eat so many sweets!

check2.q: Your friend feels sad. Which is good advice?
options: You should talk to a grown-up you trust.
You should keep it a secret forever.

Keeping sad feelings inside doesn't help. Talking does!
Telling someone kind is a good idea, so this is bad advice.

check2.explain: Talking to a grown-up you trust is good advice.
check2.say: Your friend feels sad. Which is good advice?

lessons.grown: 👪 should / shouldn't + bare infinitive for advice and opinions (A2 Key); What should I…? to ask for advice. Softer than must (the previous lesson): advice, not a rule. Common errors: should to, shoulds, he should goes.

lessons.title: me, him, her, them
lessons.art_alt: Gumdrop, a mint gumdrop pet with a leaf on top, holds a basket of presents; Sumi the fox in a chef hat already holds a pink gift, and Puffbun, a white fluffy pet in a chef hat, smiles while she waits for hers

hook.text: It's the Candy Village bake-off, and Gumdrop is giving out prize presents! Sumi already has her pink gift. Puffbun is smiling, waiting for hers. But Gumdrop's list is muddled: “Give the pink gift to she. Give a gift to he.” That sounds funny! Can you fix Gumdrop's list?
hook.say: It's the Candy Village bake-off, and Gumdrop is giving out prize presents! Sumi already has her pink gift. Puffbun is smiling, waiting for hers. But Gumdrop's list is muddled: “Give the pink gift to she. Give a gift to he.” That sounds funny! Can you fix Gumdrop's list?

discover.text: Who gets a present? Drag the right word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: A girl → her. A boy → him. Two or more → them. Yourself → me.

items.s: Sumi has a pink gift. Gumdrop gave it to ___.
items.why: Sumi is a girl: Gumdrop gave it to her.

items.s: Puffbun says, “Is there a gift for ___?”
items.why: Puffbun means herself: a gift for me.

items.s: Hoot is here too. Gumdrop has a gift for ___.
items.why: Hoot is a boy: a gift for him.

items.s: The twins are clapping. Gumdrop waves at ___.
items.why: Two friends: Gumdrop waves at them.

items.s: Crumb is hungry. Let's give ___ a cookie!
items.why: Crumb is a boy: give him a cookie.

discover.say: Who gets a present? Drag the right word into each gap, or tap it.

rule.text: Words like I, he, she, we and they sit at the front and do the action: She gives a gift. After the doing word, or after to, for or with, they change: I becomes me, he becomes him, she becomes her, we becomes us, they becomes them. Gumdrop gives a gift to her. Hoot waves at them.
examples: Give the gift to me, please!
Sumi loves her gift. Gumdrop gave it to her.
Hoot and Crumb are here. Let's play with them.
rule.say: Words like I, he, she, we and they sit at the front and do the action: She gives a gift. After the doing word, or after to, for or with, they change: I becomes me, he becomes him, she becomes her, we becomes us, they becomes them. Gumdrop gives a gift to her. Hoot waves at them.
sayEx: Give the gift to me, please!
Sumi loves her gift. Gumdrop gave it to her.
Hoot and Crumb are here. Let's play with them.

check.q: Hoot is my friend. I like ___ a lot.

notes.he: He sits at the front. After like, use him.
notes.his: His is for things Hoot has, like his glasses. Here: like him.

check.explain: After like: I like him.
check.say: Hoot is my friend. I like blank a lot.

check.q: Puffbun and Sumi are coming. Let's wait for ___.

notes.they: They sits at the front. After for, use them.
notes.their: Their is for things they have, like their hats. Here: for them.

check.explain: After for: wait for them.
check.say: Puffbun and Sumi are coming. Let's wait for blank.

check.q: Which sentence is right?
options: Gumdrop gave a gift to me.
Gumdrop gave a gift to I.
Gumdrop gave a gift to my.

I sits at the front: I got a gift. After to, use me.
My needs a thing after it, like my gift. Here: to me.

check.explain: After to: a gift to me.
check.say: Which sentence is right?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Each of these words has a twin. One twin sits at the front and does the action: I, he, she, we, they. The other twin waits after the action: me, him, her, us, them. So: She hugs him. He hugs her. They help us. We help them. Look where the word sits, then pick the right twin.
examples: 👯 I → me · he → him · she → her
🤗 She hugs him. He hugs her.

discover.text: Is the right twin in each sentence? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.
discover.hint: At the front: I, he, she, we, they. After the action: me, him, her, us, them.

items.why: After waved at: him. That's right.
After helped, she becomes her: Gumdrop helped her.
At the front, use he: He is my best friend.
After with: them. That's right.
After hugged, I becomes me: Puffbun hugged me.
After help: us. That's right.

discover.say: Is the right twin in each sentence? Drag each card or tap it, then tap a box.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Each of these words has a twin. One twin sits at the front and does the action: I, he, she, we, they. The other twin waits after the action: me, him, her, us, them. So: She hugs him. He hugs her. They help us. We help them. Look where the word sits, then pick the right twin.

check2.q: My grandma lives far away. I call ___ every Sunday.

notes.she: She sits at the front. After call, use her.
notes.hers: Hers means it belongs to her. After call: her.

check2.explain: After call: I call her.
check2.say: My grandma lives far away. I call blank every Sunday.

check2.q: Crumb and I are hungry. Can you make ___ a sandwich?

notes.we: We sits at the front. After make, use us.
notes.our: Our needs a thing after it, like our lunch. Here: make us.

check2.explain: We becomes us after the action: make us a sandwich.
check2.say: Crumb and I are hungry. Can you make blank a sandwich?

check2.q: Sumi is so kind. ___ gave me a big hug.

notes.Her: At the front, doing the action, use she.
notes.Hers: Hers means it belongs to her. At the front: she.

check2.explain: At the front, doing the action: She gave me a hug.
check2.say: Sumi is so kind. blank gave me a big hug.

lessons.grown: 👪 Subject vs object personal pronouns (A2 Key): I/me, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them (you and it stay the same); object pronouns after verbs and prepositions (to me, with them). Common errors: Me and him went…, give it to I, and mixing with possessives (his, their), which the A1 'my, your, his, her' lesson covers.
